chunks: And regarding the leg, when it breaks and is set without defect or flaw, its compensation is one-fifth of the wergild of the leg, being two hundred Dinars; and the compensation for its fracture (crack) is four-fifths of the compensation for its breaking, being one hundred and sixty Dinars; and regarding its exposure is one-quarter of the compensation for its breaking, being fifty Dinars; and regarding its piercing is half the compensation for its exposure, being twenty-five Dinars; and regarding the displacement of its bones is one-quarter of the compensation for its breaking, being fifty Dinars; and regarding its penetration is one-quarter of the compensation for its breaking, being fifty Dinars; and regarding a wound in it that does not heal is thirty-three Dinars and one-third of a Dinar. So if the leg becomes defective, its compensation is one-third of the wergild of the soul, being three hundred and thirty-three Dinars and one-third of a Dinar.

key_terms.دِيَة: Blood money or wergild (compensation for injury/death)
key_terms.صَدْع: Fracture or crack (as opposed to a complete break)
key_terms.عَثْم: Defect or flaw (specifically in the setting of a bone)

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic legal compensation for a broken or defective leg?
ai.summary: This passage from al-Kafi outlines the precise monetary compensation (diyah) for various leg injuries, distinguishing between temporary fractures and permanent defects (‘athm) based on the healing quality. It establishes a hierarchical valuation system where specific injuries like exposure or penetration are calculated as fractions of the base fracture cost, culminating in a fixed one-third share of the full soul’s wergild for a permanently maimed leg. This detailed jurisprudence reflects the Shia tradition’s emphasis on quantifiable justice in bodily harm, ensuring equitable restitution for both physical damage and functional loss.
